comments.text: The last GPU I had was a 2080ti, that was an upgrade from a 9080ti.  It wasn't that expensive, but what shocked me at the time was the power requirements and heat output.  Combine that with a 5950x and the heat output from this combo was too much for me to game comfortably for very long.  Looking at the latest from Intel and AMD and the any of the high-end GPU's and this situation is even worse today.   Linus's comment about customer moving to consoles because of the price of GPU's is partly true, but is also the utterly ridiculous power consumption and heat output that need to change.  I switched to an xbox series x and while it's not as fast as a PC, it's quiet and it was cheap, and I can run it for long gaming sessions without it pumping out a ton of heat.  The games I play like cyberpunk run quickly enough.  On a side note, while nobody would ever say the Mac is a gaming platform,  out of interest I played No Man's Sky on the base model Mac Studio and compared it to the Xbox X and it was much faster, objects on the ground rendered much quicker and made gameplay so much better.  And throughout the Mac remained silent and sips power.  So while the Mac is no gaming platform it proves that it can game and do it with very reasonable power usage and heat output, so why can't PC's do this?  For mainstream gaming to continue to prosper it has to become much, much more efficient, in terms value, power consumption and heat output.  The current trends are simply unsustainable.

comments.text:
Here is my theory for why Nvidia is pricing their cards so high. With Moore's law slowing down and games and software no longer being exponentially more difficult to run every generation, there won't be massive demand for graphics cards every year regardless of where Nvidia prices their cards.

If they price them too low, that ultimately hurts them significantly as it fills a lot of demand at a low price now, vs spreading it out over a few years at a higher price. If they overshoot demand, and have high sales this year, that also sets unrealistic expectations to investors. I think they're aiming to price in such a way where they can have consistent sales numbers year over year.

I'm betting that Nvidia looks at their pricing of the 10 series cards as a mistake, and don't want to repeat that. As you said, many people are still on that generation of cards 7 years later.

comments.text: As a 4070 ti owner who has been gaming my entire life but has not kept up with the times the last 5-7 years. I did quick research and paired a 13600k with the 4070 ti. Have had it for about 1.5 months now and have played cyberpunk, hunt, redfall, and red dead 2. All have played awesome and I couldn't be happier. I got a little nervous after I built it that I made a mistake but after using it myself and seeing some of these benchmarks I'm happy with my choices also in my opinion the best performance for power build you can get. I don't intend on using it for 4k and will likely build another in 5-7 years. In all likelihood I'll be able to max out 1440 for that amount of time without a problem and if I have to turn a texture or two down at the end of its life I will. Should it have had 16 gb for the price well yes and I'm a little disappointed about that but the cache is like 16x more than the last gen so I think people are exaggerating the ram need. Also as games get optimized after release they will get better. Overall I'm happy and just wanted to give an opinion from someone who owns one. If I had a 30 series card I might hold out till 50 series but if you're building a new pc go for it I'm happy. And people will hate on frame gen or dlss 3 but if its single player to me it looks great and feels smooth. For something competitive I would never use something like that. For example I run medium setting at 1080 on cs go with a 165hz monitor and cap my frames at 320 because it reduces latency to .6-1.2 and uses 44 w. I have a 1080 Ti that I bought in 2018 (in hindsight, an extremely wise purchase). This was just before RTX came out and the 1080 was top dog. I just don't see any reason to upgrade right now. I can get a solid 55-60 FPS in RD2 with everything cranked at 2K resolution. Even on the work side (I'm a graphic designer and do 3D rendering and video editing), it's still performing just fine. Sure the RT tech is there and getting better. But the games aren't there yet. And most of the games coming out that use it are not games I have any interest in playing (looking at you AAA games with pretty graphics and bad gameplay). It's not worth the cash right now. It's just a better financial decision to not spend the $1k now, or spend it on more "future-proof" parts of a PC, and get a new GPU in a few years when more games support RT and the tech is better. 

I've had one Radeon card ever (long, long ago; and have nothing bad to say about it). And have been with EVGA Nivida cards for... ever. I might actually look at a Radeon again the next time around, because I am one of those weird consumers who would rather buy an "inferior" product (which, I really don't think is at all fair to say about AMD) from a good company. A sidebar to the video - I sincerely hope you got better, Linus. Your voice sounds so strained in this one...

[edit] on the video - if Moore's law is dead, then charging the same for less would be hard, charging more for less would be near impossible. I looked up a vew reviews and metrics. In the process I extrapolated that their 4xxx products seem to compete with their own 2xxx and 3xxx products in performance, but not in price. Yes, there is the raytracing and the more modern encoder, but those are NOT good enough to justify a 200usd+ price hike at msrp. Buff that up for the partner profit and the cards become completely asinine in their pricing. They are obviously holding back the release of the 4060 and lower, to cover for the fact that they sneakily changed the numbers on their entire lineup. What should've been a 4060 in performance gain with respect to the 3060, is now a 4070ti. What should've been a 4070 with respect to 3070, is not 4080... we are yet to see anything in the lower segment, like 4030s, 4050s. Something tells me these would be so laughably bad, noone would want to buy them new... kinda how noone seems to be eager about giving nVidia the ridiculous price tag they're asking for. I remember a video done by either LTT or GN or maybe Jay, can't remember, where you folks (as tech medias) did say that nVidia has no choice but to price these things at these price points due to investors and share holders. Would love to hear your honest opinion on whether there is an actual way to get this situation back to relative normality, without hurting anybody. Can we get the millionaires and billionaires their yachts, while keeping the humble gamer from dropping 800usd+ for a gpu, when the same caliber gpu would've set the buyer back by 400usd 10 years ago. I know it's not 10 years ago, but we have also not seen two times the salary increases in the first world.

While the cost might be relatively similar to produce these modern GPUs as it were 10 years ago, they know they can't keep improving them that much every generation as easily as they used to.

So we are in some sort of GPU duopoly, where they are aware that, if they significantly drop their prices and people buy the latest ones "cheap" now, they won't be buying the expensive ones 2-4 years down the line, since there won't be that big of a difference to justify upgrading.

comments.text: People need to realize that this is a bad purchase. The average consumer won't care, but the techie people will. For starters, one of the major issues with the 4070 Ti is the gimped 192-Bit memory bus. The 3070 came with a 256-Bit bus, and that extra bandwidth matters! Also, a 3070 costs only $500-$600 now. A 192- Bit bus that 3060 uses, and you're paying $800+ for that! Ok, so why the 192-Bit Bus then? Easy... Profit! Why? Hear me out. The performance you're seeing from the 4070 Ti is with DLSS 3.0 enabled... A software trick to give you more frames. The thing is, I'd rather have the pure raw bandwidth of a 256 Bit-Bus that can be used on ALL GAMES. DLSS is pretty game specific. Having a trimmed down bus means you're going to have performance problems with other games, or be no better than the 30 series offerings!! I'm hanging onto my 3070 and it's raw 256-Bit bus. Why would I pay $800.00 just to get 4 extra gigs of ram, that is essentially wasted unless you're trying to game at 4K, A little better ray tracing, (I don't really care about Ray Tracing, nor do any of my games support it) some AV1 encoder, and a DLSS 3.0 game specific "Cheat to simulate more frames through hackery"?? No, folks, you're paying too much for a card that should be $450.00. I am forced to wait for the 5000 series, or see what AMD/Intel has up their sleeve. Look past the DLSS BS and see what you're actually getting! You're getting ripped off!

comments.text:
@zortlak  Not only that, the economics of the situation are likely the biggest reason the 1000 series will remain the ultimate value upgrade, forever.

1. Planar node to FinFet
The 10 series was the last nvidia GPU on a planar node, which has significantly less manufacturing cost and complexity than a more powerful FinFet node, like the one AMD were using at the time.
2. Architecture
The 10 series was one of Nvidia's greatest accomplishments in terms of architecture. AMD at the time had a superior node, but their engineers could not design a more efficient architecture, even with a more efficient manufacturing process. Nvidia's maxwell not only crushed AMD's polaris in efficiency and cost, but also in performance.
3. Node Size
The 10 series had an unusually small 80 class chipset, because it was all that was required to completely invalidate AMD's offerings at the time. This allowed Nvidia to create monsters like the titan who had the full die area unlocked, for the enthusiasts, and sell cheaper GPU's that performed better at cheaper prices to the masses.

comments.text:
Guys, the problem is that there is no single price that they can give. 
Abstractly, the ideal would be them giving the price that you would pay. 
1. Prices are different by region
2. Prices fluctuate over time, because of anything from day-to-day sales to geopolitical events
3. MSRP is just that: Manufacturer Suggested Retail Price.
All three of those first words have issues:

3.1 - The manufacturers set this, and they don’t necessarily have to set it at the econ 101 ideal where supply meets demand in a perfectly competitive market; they control supply.

3.2 - It’s just a suggestion, the retailers ultimately charge what they will

3.3 - This is the retail, i.e. new, price

4 - Used prices are not just unpredictable, but unknowable. There isn’t data on what price every used card sold at; you can’t even assume the prices that you see on buy-n-sell sites because there is very probably bartering that doesn’t get seen, let alone made available by the few sites that attempt to show their sale histories

5 - Cards aren’t as fungible as we assume; 

5.1 - Used cards are obviously worth less than new.  And even within those, “true value” is affected by things like how much warranty the card has, intensity of use, previous operating environment, whether it comes with receipt, or was mined on, or overclocked, or cleaned regularly, comes with box and cords, etc etc

5.2 New card prices might include separate value adds, like bundled games or extra retailer warranty

And the kicker is that we who might want to be surgical about price with things like price/performance are more likely in a segment where buying used makes sense, and used has the least universally knowable data


A - There are sources that try to present price/performance numbers like UserBenchmark and others, and there’s good reason why nobody in the comments recomended them to you. Go look, the data’s shit.
comments.author: @blazerorb

comments.text:
@blazerorb  First, yes, I agree there are all sorts of variables to what a card will actually cost, so it's pointless to try and give that picture.

The thing is that MSRP is actually more useful than any real time price you might encounter. I agree that MSRP isn't legally binding but it sets the expectations in the market that are then adjusted by all the other factors. We actually see NVIDIA using this as a tool to bleed card manufacturers dry in all the shenanigans EVGA decided not to deal with. Set the MSRP low enough and board partners won't have the headroom in margins to stand out bith better quality without looking greedy by making an "excessively expensive" card

But, much more importantly than all that (even more important than what you the individual will wind up paying), it illustrates the mindset of a manufacturer and how much they respect you and your money. Especially if adjusted for inflation price per performance can easily illustrate when a company is trying to give you a fair exchange of value, or when thinks that you should pay them more because they don't respect the value of your time and resources.

And don't say that this is not the case, I'm not just inventing this. GN has already used this metric multiple times to illustrate a company's bad behavior in the past to great effect. My hope was to advance the presence of the metric to make it easier to understand and more commonly seen.

comments.text:
So, looking at this today, the 4070ti is readily available at MSRP (MSI Ventus for $799). I ordered one, it is on the way.  Looking at NewEgg, it's still there, still available, at that price.  There are an assortment of others at various prices, but all are more or less in line with the MSRP.  I haven't seen anything (apart from a few LOLZ outliers) even closely resembling the prices we've seen for the 30 series over the past year or so.

So, with that confirmed, we look at where this card rests within the product stack, and where others have over the previous two generations:

2080 (base): $700
3080 (base, 10gb model): $800
4070ti: $800

Those are the comparable cards from those generations, in my opinion at least, fairly close to the date of the original product line launch (that means no "Super" from the 20 series, and no 3080 12gb, because both of those came quite a bit later in that line's life-cycle, and the 4070ti is just a couple months out from the OG release of the 4080).

I feel like people are getting really tripped up by the model numbers instead of looking at the intent of the product (and maybe Nvidia's marketing is to blame too, as the message does seem to be inconsistent at times). This card is meant to be an elite option for 1440p gamers (even though it actually does quite well at 4k).  *From what I remember*, as well as what I experienced as a 2080 Super owner, the 2080 and 3080 were both that as well---presented as a high end option for 1440p gaming.  The 3090/ti and the 2080ti (and the Titan if you wanted to go really crazy) were intended to be the 4k cards.

And if that's the case---and real world experience suggests it is---this pricing is in line with what we should expect based on the previous 2 generations.  Even if you go back to the 10 series---arguably the largest single generation jump ever, depending on what you're looking at---the GTX 1080, which was absolutely intended to be a 1440p option (with the TI model aimed at people who wanted TOP END 1440p performance and even venture into 4k)---was priced at $599 *six years ago*.

Yes, the 4070ti was originally branded a 4080, and I get why people are angry because it wasn't entirely above-board, but when you look at the whole map...that's kind of what it IS.

Even if we throw MSRP for the 30 series out the window---which we can only do on paper---this thing easily beats the 3080 10gb, beats the 3080ti, somewhat tops the 3090 base, and swaps blows with the 3090ti, and it does so for (at worst) equal money (in the case of the 3080 10gb) or (at best) around 60% of the money (the original MSRP on the 3090ti).


So exactly what is everyone mad about? Does anyone honestly not think this card is solidly positioned, robustly featured, and fairly priced given the reality of this hobby right now?  A 12.5% bump ($100) in 3 1/2 years is too much to take?  Don't look at the 3070, that's not what this thing is aimed at.  It obliterates that card.  It isn't supposed to be the successor to it. Nvidia really wasn't entirely off-base calling it a 4080 12gb.  This card is the logical successor to the 1080, 2080, and 3080.

Anyway, if all the bitter bros wanna sit on their 10 series cards and claim some kind of moral victory, and get stuck in another 2 year product shortage, have at it.  I ordered one of these at MSRP---AND I SAY AGAIN THEY ARE STILL OBTAINABLE AT THAT PRICE---and I feel really, really good about that purchase.

Cheers.

Edited for clarity.

comments.text:
I think if you've got a healthy build going, it can be easy to demonize Nvidia, but...
If you own an older video card & are looking to upgrade, let's consider this:

Radeon 7900 XT - $900 on Amazon.
RTX 4070 Ti - $850 on Amazon.

While rasterization and raw performance are important, who the Hell is buying 30 and 40 series cards, without considering Ray-tracing as a measurement of performance?
In addition to that, who isn't considering DLSS or FSR as a measurement of performance?

If you want to call them gimmicks (largely debatable), EVERYONE got suckered in. 
Until these gimmicks become less important, I think Rasterization, sadly, might have to take a back seat for a little while. 
If you factor in these "gimmicks" with performance and market share values, the 4070 Ti is good. It's $40 cheaper than AMD's current equivalent.

BUT EVEN from a pure rasterization standpoint, the 4070 Ti still beats out ALMOST the 30 series entirely and its average FPS is 120+ in 4K - that's nothing to laugh about.

comments.text: @gibusosu9304  Given the 3900x is still better than 87% cpu's out there, it was not a bottleneck in my testing.. comments.text:
@Kungpaoshizzi  Regarding code efficiency, I'd like to add. Right now CPU and GPUs have progressed sooo fast in recent years. Even if utilization is 100%, Most of the time CPU keeps waiting for next chunk from memory.

We're now getting limited back by cache and bandwidth. 
3090 had 6MB L2 cache, 
4090 has 72 MB L2 cache.

That's the actual difference, 3090 itself is so fast that physical bandwidth is holding it back. AMD worked on cache and optimising compute in Ryzen and Navi.

For code efficiency, GPU will be about Software + Hardware as we're seeing with DLSS/FSR. We'll get more improvements in software part.

comments.text:
@5226-p1e  It's called "optimizing" also known as "turning down the detail levels through ini files instead of options".

When GTA5 released on the PS4, the game ran between 16-30fps, with an average of 27fps. It was freaking TERRIBLE. What did they do? They simply released a patch that basically removed 50% of all shadows, drew the remaining 50% in far lower resolution, and turned down the texture detail and a plethora of other things in order to get the game running at a constant 30fps. That's not a TRICK, it's barely even TWEAKING the code. It's basically turning down settings.

Back in the day, Quake came with very few visual options and ran slowly on pretty much any PC out there, except the best of the best PC. But you could edit command line prompts and cfg files and use the console to remove detail settings further and speed the game up. Turning down settings. Not tweaking. They come with a visual impact. Same with resolution scaling in modern drivers, for example. Sure FSR or DSR will be used to sharpen up (anti-alias) those jaggies, giving the impression that the game ISN'T running at a much lower resolution, but it IS running at a much lower resolution. 

The question is, do the extra fps give more benefit than the drop in fidelity?

Like I said - the 970 was a formidable mid range card for many years. But it's days are long gone. Try to find a second hand 580, they are so cheap these days, and offer way better performance. OR even better, grab a 5600XT if you can find one. Faster than a GTX1080 in many modern titles and I see them selling for under £170 on the used market.

comments.text:
​ @Gundwn  Box/Whisker plots [1] and violin plots [2] are the default way to represent density data on a one dimensional axis (1.5 in case of violin plots, but whatever, the bars have a width as well). The frame timings collected with one benchmark run are one example of such density data. The current presentation shows three points of the thousands available in the data. I'll try my best to explain to you why this data is density data and what advantage the other plots provide. If you're not interested, skip the explanations, but please at least look at "examples" and "Why it matters" at the end of this comment.

Why frame timing data is density data and therefore a prime candidate for such plots:
Simplified: There may be 1 frame that took 20ms, 4 that took 18 and 100 that took 15ms. These would be the values of the three bar lines shown in the current presentation. But in real data you'd have 20 frames that took 14ms. They are not presented in the visualization. This data is lost between measurement and presentation.
Advanced, more accurate explanation: For an actual run you will have a frame count for each ms value, or for every 0.1 or 0.01 ms timing, whatever precision the PC records the frame timings with. This is density data, because you are able to look at one frame time (e.g. 15ms) and count how many frames during the run were withing say +-1ms of that value. For example look at 15ms and you will see that for a game that runs at 60fps 90% of frames took between 14 and 16 ms to render. The density of frame time data is high for 15ms. But look at 20ms and only 1% of all frames took 19-21ms to render, the density of frame timings is low around the 20ms value. Maybe see [5] for a visual guide to this explanation. [5] is considered in more detail at the end of this comment.

What the current presentation doesn't show:
A single run will record thousands of frames and how long they took to render. Condensing the data down to three values removes a lot of information. We know the average, low 5% and low 1%. But what about the 99% high? The 0.1% low? The 50% low (the median, which probably differs from the mean)?

What other plots would show:
The other plots show a lot more information. A Box plot [1] shows the the three quartiles (25, 50, 75% low) and, depending on the whisker mode used, also the min/max, standard deviation, 10% and 90% or 1% and 99% low/high. An additional mark can be added to show the mean. As you can see this is much more information than the three data points provided by the currently used bar plot.
A violin plot [2] would show even more information, providing insight into the full distribution of recorded frame timings. The exact method used to construct the displayed curve can vary, depending on the smoothing parameter used in the kernel density estimator ([6], but the details there are not necessary to understand). They can be combined with box plots to give a lot of information about a complex distribution at once.

Examples to show what the difference would be:
In order to help with the intuition about the differences, consider some examples from other topics:
a) population demographics of your country. Take for example Canada (because Linus) [3]. It's not very helpful to know that the 1% low is ~0.5 years, the 5% low is 5 years and the median is 41 years. You have no idea if that is a good or bad population distribution, if there are enough workers to support the old and young people. The usual way to represent this data is instead with a population pyramid, [4] which is approximately equal to a violin plot.
b) income distribution. Knowing the 1% low, 5% low and average of yearly income/earnings is not enough to tell if the income is fairly distributed or not. With only these three data points you have no idea about the income of the top 10%, 1%, 0.1% and can not reason about, say, additional taxes for the super rich. Both Whisker and Violin plots would help and show more of the important information.

Why it matters:
Consider two theoretical GPUs. Both produce 1% lows at 50 fps, 5% lows at 60 fps and an average at 120 fps. Indistinguishable with the bar plot method. But it is entirely possible, that one GPU produces 1% of frames at 50 fps, 49.5% at 60 fps and 49.5% of frames at 180 fps while the other produces 1% of frames at 50 fps, 4% at 60 fps and 95% of frames at ~120 fps. They look identical on the bar graph, but are clearly very very different. Sure, real GPU data will look more evenly distributed ... until it doesn't:  
Take a look at the Gamers Nexus Arc GPU video [5], where GN explicitly shows the frame timings of the Arc driver across a run, because the three bars did not get the point across. Just imaging the data shown in [5] to be compressed to the left of the graph, as if the pixels of the line plot were free to move and gravity pushed them to the left. They would accumulate in a big blob for the AMD card, but not for the Arc GPU. Such problems would be readily evident in a violin plot, even if the 1 and 5% low were identical.

Links, well yes but actually no. Youtube hates comments with links and likes to delete comments linking to more information. So you'll have to copy paste to google yourself. 
[1]: Wikipedia: Box Plot
[2]: Wikipedia: Violin plot
[3]: Google: "Canada's population estimates, third quarter 2022" > first result > tables > "Population estimates on July 1st, by age and sex"
[4]: Wikipedia: Population pyramid
[5]: Gamers Nexus: "Intel Arc A750 Limited Edition GPU Review & Benchmarks vs. AMD RX 6600, A770, & More" at 9min 55s
[6]: Wikipedia: Kernel Density Estimation

comments.text:
This card is about the same performance as the RTX 3080 and RX 6800 XT.  If nVidia had released it as an RTX 4080, then there would have been a generational uplift of about ZERO PERCENT despite costing $200 more.  Way to go nVidia, way to go!

I don't understand how people (meaning the people at Linus Tech Tips) are ONLY NOW discovering that, at the same price point, a Radeon card will absolutely destroy a GeForce card in gaming.  This is based on my own experience with Radeon cards that began in 2008 but I do know that it has been true since nVidia released the GeForce 8800 GTX.  Linus worked at NCIX around the same time that I worked at Tiger Direct so I don't get how he didn't see this sooner.

I remember back when nVidia first changed its numbering scheme from "4-digit number and suffix" to "prefix and 3-digit number", something that was perfectly demonstrated when they renamed the GeForce 9800 GTX+ as the GeForce GTS 250.  In early June of 2008, nVidia released the GTX 260 to much fanfare.  IIRC, the fanfare was because the GTX 260 was the first single card that could run Crysis so the fanfare was deserved.  However, the price on it was...suspiciously steep.  Many of my Tiger Direct co-workers were GeForce 8800 GTX-owning fanboys and had no qualms about pushing these cards onto customers.  However, I knew that ATi was going to release their answer to the GTX 260 in less than two weeks.  Their answer to the GTX 260 892MB was the Radeon HD 4870 1GB.

The HD 4870 proved to be ever so slightly faster but we're talking about a difference so insignificant that I just considered them to be on par with each other.  The difference was like 3%, about the same as the difference between the RTX 3080 and RX 6800 XT so it's not like it was mind-blowing by any means.  However, that's when I REALLY saw the power of ATi.  The two cards essentially traded blows in performance but there was a shocking difference in the pricing of the two cards (prices in Canadian dollars):
GTX 260 892MB - $600
HD 4870 1GB - $350

I honestly wondered what was wrong with the people who were paying $250 MORE for a card that was no faster than a card that cost just over half.  The HD 4870 was fantastic.  So good in fact, that I bought a second for Crossfire and they worked amazingly well.  Since that day, ALL of my video cards have been Radeons because I don't buy halo cards and at the price points that mere mortals can pay, Radeons were always faster cards.

This is not exactly news, this is how it has been for at least sixteen years.  It just serves to show how little attention most people pay when it comes to what they're throwing their money at.

comments.text:
This is how markets crash. People get high on profit, selling to the highest bidder (credit card companies, investors, scalpers, other middlemen, etc.) who is equally high, thinking they can just wipe off the cost with the next idiot who will pay them even more. They forget that at the end of the day, the consumer is the pillar that holds the industry up, and they push a little too hard on that pillar, and it breaks. 

Then the consumers can't pay, so the creditors can't pay, so the middlemen can't pay, and before you know it the whole market has collapsed.

We've been through this more than enough times in the 21st century; I'm kinda tired of it at this point.

It sounds like something you'd say to a 10 year old, but the whole world literally depends on treating each other with just enough respect to keep us attached to each other. The economy is just a reflection of that.

something nvidia seems to keep overlooking when it comes to their overreliance on RayTracing in performance graphs, is that unlike previous generations (pascal and maxwell especially), mid-tier 50 and 60 series cards keep coming out significantly later than the 80 and 90 cards (and especially with 20 series, had poor if any DLSS/RT performance, made worse by the 50 and 60 cards standing to benefit from DLSS the most), even though the 50 and 60 cards are historically purchased by a lot more people

edit: I actually appreciate that LTT is taking note of the RayTracing usage problems, because reviews in the last couple years often placed Nvidia cards over AMD cards because of RayTracing performance, even when the equivalent AMD card had comperable if not better rasterization performance (what the vast majority of people and games will actually use, at least for the foreseeable future. and as we all know, "futureproofing" is never a safe bet)

@Aphorism89  Well, there cost of the process nodes to manufacture have gone up considerably in recent years. They're kinda reaching the realistic limits of miniaturizing silicon. And the last two years have had outrageous inflation (looking at 16% for 2 years, officially, and more like 25% real world). So if a card cost $400 to $430 in early 2020, The same cards would cost $500 now, just purely based on elected officials using "printing money" as a fiscal policy.

3090/3090ti and 4090/4090ti basically take the place of the "Titan" cards of previous generations. Kind of the "money is no object, just how fast can we go?" tier. They've always been several hundred dollars more than the ___80 and under cards. Usually in the past though, a ___80 ti card, would come very close to the performance of the titan cards (or 3090/3090ti), at a much lower cost. Making the titan cards uninteresting for most consumers.

This gen though, the 4080 has a very large performance drop compared to the 4090. Does that make the 4090 fantastic? Or is the 4080 just garbage at being an ___80 card? I dunno which... both are a valid way of looking at it I think. 

But the 4090 is priced similar to 3090 or past titan cards (especially if you're allowing for inflation). Meanwhile the 4090 is just flat-out unquestionably overpriced for what it is. A particularly weak ___80 card at $1200? The 2080 tried that price point, and failed miserably at that price. And it was at least a fairly strong ___80 card, as viewed within it's generation. The 4080 is a joke at $1200.

Last time I bought a card and thought I got a good deal, it was a 1080 Ti Strix. It was before the mining craze. Paid $800 for it. But that was 5 (almost 6) years ago. And realistically just from my dollars being worth less as currency alone, that would be $1000+ today. But it was a particularly strong ___80 card. And the super-premium AIB version of it. A 4080 Strix is like $1500... which is completely disconnected from inflation, and reality. When I saw Jensen announce the price of the 4080 FE in the launch presentation, with the huge drop in performance compared to the 4090... I flipped off my monitor and said things my mother wouldn't be proud of.

The 4090 price didn't bother me as much. High, yeah. But not too outlandish for a titan/_90 card. It did make me wonder what a 4090 ti's price would get jacked up to though.

That the 4090 has better performance per dollar than the 4080, is completely nuts and stupid (or greedy to a blatantly anti-consumer degree).

If you want to say all graphics cards should be half their current price? I don't think it's realistic, but ok... then a 4090 would be $800. But if that were true, the 4080 should be $500 tops. Not $600.

@TrepidDestiny  A young lad at the school I worked at wanted a new PC - he was using an all in one and could hardly play counterstrike. I was advising him what to buy and in the end his Dad called me, and asked if I'd be willing to work with him to put together a good machine, fast but great value. The student was hell bent on a 2080, which cost around £700 at the time. I talked him out of it, for his poor Dads sake, and I almost had to force him to buy a 5700XT. At the time, it cost just £20 more than an RTX2060, but was significantly faster. It also cost around £130 less than a 2070.

Fast forward a year and a half, and that 5700XT wasn't just beating the 2070, it was beating the 2070Ti in many titles. I'm quite sure in another six months it'll be beating the 2080, which cost double what his Dad paid for that 5700XT.

This is why I find it endlessly funny when people are buying the inferior, slower 3060Ti en masse rather than the 6700XT. Not only is the AMD card faster (sometimes a lot faster), in 12 months it'll be beating the 3070, and in a year it'll be matching the 3070Ti ... a card which is twice as expensive. But still, people go with the worse product, filling Nvidias pockets, and hindering AMD's R&D and motivation to even bother competing, in a market flooded with absolute moron consumers.

Rather than good-bad-good-bad the cycle starting with the 10-series is more like kinda bad-really bad-bad-terrible.
Sure there is oscillation, but the trend is not flat, it's down. 
When we see 70-class cards at $425 and 60-class cards at $275, then we can call it a truly good generation.
60-class in this case is defined as top-tier performance from two generations back (see 1060 vs 780ti, 960 vs 680, 760 vs 580 etc) and 70-tier as last gen top tier performance (1070 vs 980ti, 970 vs 780ti, 770 vs 680 etc).
Anything less than that is simply a continuation of the downward trend we've seen since 2016.

Well done review. Probably your best yet, as everyone so far as said, for sure. 

My takeaways from this review: First, unless you have an extreme fear of planned obsolescence, and expect NVIDIA to poison pill their 3090 series of cards, just stick with the 3090 series.

Second, I am reminded of a story a sales agent told me once when I bought a 2016 Nissan Altima. I noticed that it looked more like my 2007 model and not as high end as the 2014 model that I owned before that. The agent basically said that they noticed that with the look of the 2014 models, Nissan saw a dip in the sales of the Maxima series, because they looked very similar, by redesigning and making it more like an upscaled Sentra, they were able to get course correct their sales on the Maxima. It appears that the 4000 series was supposed to be NVIDIA's Maxima, but they priced it at the Infiniti price point, but through Altima parts under the hood in the case of the 4070 TI, while their 3090 has some Maxima parts. They need to take a step back, and decide what they are making for the next model of their cards, and NOT gamble on the fact that just because consumer did it during the pandemic that we will continue to do so, because we are fickle.

IE: It was left "Empty" for a reason. 

Of course having a small motorcycle radiator block as a heat sink will result in better thermals, but there's a reason why we're not strapping automotive levels of metal to electronics, several in fact as I mentioned. Because it's not the only component that likes to get cool air, vent hot air, or needs cooling tubes unkinked and unobstructed.

And it's not "Better cooling and quieter" When every single one coil and cap whines like hell due to the out of control power consumption, transient power spike issues and more.

Did anybody question the sorting method for the GPUs in these graphs? NVIDIA seems to only be interested in targeting the high end market, regardless of what they're actually delivering.  They are ignoring - at their peril - that most of the monitors on sale are still 1080p, and maybe 1440p, not 4k.  If you want 4k at 60+ FPS, then you're going to pay the money for the high-end GPU.  Enjoy your card and  have fun.  The rest of us don't have that amount of disposable income but we still deserve quality, reliable hardware that is fairly spec'ed and priced.

The lower tiered SKUs should NOT be expected to do anything more than 1080p-1440p, and their prices should reflect that.  There should still be a 4050 and 4060 lineup for around $299-399 - NOT $850.  The market is there, but what NVIDIA is showing us is that they don't want to give up enough profit margin to make that happen.

This is why Intel succeeding in the market with a mid-range, affordable GPU is essential, and why I will be buying an Arc GPU for my next rig - despite their acknowledged driver/firmware weirdness.  I figure hell, I've been beta-testing Windows for years, this should be no different...

comments.text:
I disagree that consoles like the PS5 or XBSX are going to be Nvidia’s main competition, rather I believe their main competition is everything else that’s come before it. As old as 1000 series GPUs are, they are still more than capable of playing the vast majority of all games, whether it’s through emulation or PC native. 
   There’s just no logical incentive to upgrade just to play a small selection of games that require high end hardware, and that’s ignoring both the fluctuating quality of those games and the comically high price barrier. Even the PS5 and the XBSX themselves are suffering from the fact that their previous generation versions have a dedicated library on top of continuously being supported; in terms of sales, the XBSX has only just gotten around to reaching the GameCube, and the PS5 is still behind the Atari 2600, which is shockingly low considering the gaming community of today is exponentially larger than when either of those two consoles came out.
   I really think we’re closing in on an era in technology where, regardless of modern advances, the vast majority of people are fine with what they have. Anything new now has to be both incredibly accessible (i.e., cheap) and useful in a novel way to break the mold, doing the exact same thing but better doesn’t seem to be very sustainable.

Just get a 3070 or 3080 from the second-hand market, maybe even a 3090 if you get really lucky somewhere. There is no way you can make a reasonable argument for the nonsense pricing on the 3000 series and 4000 series on the main market. Or I would advise you wait until the next generation of cards and see if you can pick up a 4000 series one as some people will be dumping them for replacements. The 2070 super is still a really good card and you don't need to upgrade it for many generations. I ran a GTX 1070 until a few months ago and it has done a wonderful job, even pulling above 60 fps in Cyberpunk on medium settings in some areas. 

The only reason you'd really want to upgrade is if you want the new features, such as DLSS 3.0, or better RTX framerates as the 3000 series is a large upgrade to the 2000 series in terms of RTX performance. There's no reason to get a 4000 card unless you just have way too much money, or if you for some obscure reason really need the ridiculous performance, such as if you run a render farm or something otherwise computationally expensive. For gaming? Just stick to what you have or find something on the second hand market. Best advise I can give at least.

comments.text: I'm considering an upgrade over a six year old laptop with a 10-series card after some recent problems have me worried it will last more than a few months less than I had expected, so I had the 3060 in my eye. Seeing the difference in performance between a 3060 and a 3090ti or 4070ti in your charts has me reconsidering that. I probably wouldn't go for a 3090ti on performance alone because of how expensive they are, but the 4070ti seems like it might be a reasonable choice given it's feature set and the work I intend to use my computer for. The lower memory bandwidth has me a bit worried for multitasking, but it seems okay so long as I'm not working with 4k rendering. I would generally do 1080p, so that leaves a bit of extra room compared to the results from your 1440p benchmarks. All of the other tests, in my non-hardware expert opinion, seemed to be within a reasonable margin. Getting nearly triple the performance over a 3060 with additional features and a lower power draw compare to the 3090ti and other 40 series cards makes it seem like a great choice. I would certainly appreciate a lower MSRP, but in the current market I'm just happy to not have to pay around US$1,500. I'm finding 3060 cards for around CAD$550 right now, so if the 4090ti cards end up releasing around CAD$1,100 then I might have to choose one of those instead. When I think about the lifetime I could expect to get out of each card as performance demands increase it's hard to not see it as a better deal.

Love Linus reviews. But just here it's: "How we make excuse for RDNA3 cards? Oh, we know, lets test it without RT... and without DLSS 3.0 on 40 series". But turn on RT, and 4070ti already will put 7900XTX to shame. Not mentioning DLSS 3.0
And i am sorry, but Raytaing is future. No matetr if gamers still haven't catched on, because game developers DO WANT to work with raytracing, instead of rasterized lighting. Specifically RTGI. It's fracture of work to be done for devs, with overall way higher fidelity! (compared to older technique)
Yes, devs still holded down by publishers like Sony, forcing devs to make games to be able to run on older PS4 consoles. So devs someimes just drop RT completely (like in Horizon Forbidden West and God of War Ragnarok), since they are forced to make make first standart rasterized lighting in first place. And RTGI have to be implemented completely separately.
But eventually there simply will be no games released for PS4, meaning ABSOLUTELY ALL games will be made with RTGI only. And when that will happen - you surely will want card most optimised for raytracing. So... 30 series, or even better 40 series.

If i would want new GPU right now- i definitely would look into 4070ti (although probbaly would wait for 4070, likely will be even betetr deal performance/price-wise). For now i am still happy with my 3070.

comments.text:
Wow, didn't expect this comment to get so many likes!

I'm seeing a few comments repeated so I'll answer them here instead of individually replying:
"I can't notice the difference": Great! You have the luxury of not longing after a system powerful enough to do RT. Personally I find the difference quite dramatic, especially in games like Control  as well as Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart.

"Can the PS5 even do ray tracing?": Yes, it can! It will often not be on a very high quality preset compared to what PC can offer but then it can also do RT at playable (and for the most part stable) frame rates @ upscaled 4K.

"What was wrong with your PC/5700?": Nothing, I should have made this point clearer in my OP: I haven't switched to console, I've just gotten a console in addition to my PC. One of the reasons was RT but there were others I didn't go in to, like wanting to play some games on a 55" OLED instead of a 27" IPS and also wanting to play exclusives like TLOU. So the cost of current GPUs were one factor out of many but definitely a big one!

"The console is only cheap(er) because of the higher price of games": Partly true, consoles are definitely subsidised by game sales but that being said the hardware itself is also cheaper since it's bought in bulk and relatively underpowered to cards like the 4070Ti. Also I won't be buying every game on console, only ones I want to play with RT on the TV so it would take a long time for the price to equal a current Nvidia GPU with those same games bought on PC.

Phew, I think that's everything. Probably almost nobody will even read this since it's a super long reply to a comment but whatever 🤷‍♂️

Simple answer, Nvidia has been producing graphics chips for 25 years with known major flaws in them. They have been caught multiple times lying about their performance. I have ran into so many problems with their drivers, I just won't deal with their cards anymore. I will not buy NVidia.

AMD on the other hand has had decent cards. Their drivers have never been as bad as some people think. They definitely haven't been as efficient at times, but if programs were properly written, they would generally work fine. ATI/AMD had a huge problem for a while where companies would use proprietary extended calls that were nVidia specific and wouldn't test their products on the AMD cards. This caused AMD to have to implement their version of some of these extended calls. It got so bad that Microsoft got rid of custom extensions in later DirectX versions. Microsoft said that certain companies were using custom extended calls for stuff that there were already standard API calls for.

comments.text:
Not trying to defend Nvidia or anything .
Their prices are shit , and there no going around that.

But the percentage of people using RayTracing is irrelevant to show it’s “importance”
Because it’s not a matter of “they don’t want to”
It’s a matter of “they CAN’T”

Let me put an example that makes it clear:

Let’s imagine that we lived in a world where GPUs can’t handle Antialiasing .
Which is something we all use , specially in lower resolution.
Anti aliasing is a must!

But if most gpus couldn’t handle it,  Most people would play with out Antialiasing.

That’s the situation with Raytracing.
It’s not that people don’t want it.
It is that they don’t even know if they want it or not.
Because either their GPU can’t handle it , or it runs at “cinematic” fps so hard to appreciate how good something looks , when you are getting sub 30 fps.
As a graphic designer I know how visually changing RayTracing is to game.
And it really frustrates me to see the general ignorance surrounding it.
And big channels contributing to this ignorance. Making it look like if Raytracing was some sort of thing that Nvidia came up with.

Raytracing is a concept that existed even before Nvidia was founded as a company.

And that is going to completely revolutionize video game graphics.
In fact on movies cgi it has been a most for over 10 years already 

That’s why despite Nvidia’s bullshit, I still go team green when choosing GPU.
AMD not properly addressing the importance of Raytracing makes them IRRELEVANT for me.
Conceptually speaking , in reality they did improved their RT performance.
But still not giving it the importance it deserves .

comments.text:
ok, the idea is a VR or surround image exercise (specifically cycling) rig which can be used for winter training or just fun.
Specifics.  
You are going to want something called a smart trainer / smart turbo trainer and any normal cycle (road bike tends to work best)
A rubber backed mat to put the bike and turbo on (unless you want sweat patches on your carpet
A pc that will allow you to connect multiple monitors or multiple projectors to give an immersive wraparound feel
a couple of fans for your own comfort as you will get very hot.

The idea is to create some type of frame work with your bike/trainer combo in the middle, the screens in front and to the side of you and the pc wherever (not important).
There are several programs/apps that will allow you to cycle in a virtual world - controlling an on screen avatar based on how you cycle. Now these apps sync to your smart trainer to auto adjust the level of effort required  (get to a 20% gradient hill and you will know it).  

Specific software.
Zwift.   This is probably the most well known platform. Whilst it does host some real world locations (London, NYC, Paris, Yorkshire, Innusbruck for example) many of the cycle routes are made up worlds where you might cycle past a dinosaur or through an active volcano. Zwift however is very community based (you can have a companion app on your phone which allows you to chat to other riders around the world whilst cycling or use ingame powerups (such as lose 50% of your rider weight without having to get of the bike and use mouse/keyboard on the main pc.  You will find that a lot of pro cyclists and triathletes use zwift (I've been fortunate enough to run and cycle a few times with lionel sanders, jan frodeno and mo farah on zwift)

Rouvy.  Similar to Zwift but loads more real world routes (literally hundreds of locations around the world, from the Dolomites in Italy, to South Africa.  Rouvy is more geared towards cycling than a social interaction with exercise like zwift

Both will give you a free trial

You could build a dual setup, sign up for two trial user accounts and then two staff, or yourself and someone could literally both connect, go to the same course/route and literally race each other in real time.

hope that makes sense

comments.text:
More and more, over time, the names (and prices) are designed to confuse us. 4070 ti sits somewhere around the 3090/ti, which had a pretty high MSRP, meaning this is super good, right? It's punching in a weight class not one but potentially TWO tiers above the last gen? Except we're already forgetting that anything above the 3080 was a ripoff in terms of price and performance. 3080 ti was barely better than a 3080, 3090 barely better than that, 3090 ti barely better again... what, like a total 15~20% performance increase all the way from 3080 to 3090 ti in most games? And the MSRPs were never meant to make sense - it was a class of card completely outside the realm of normalcy, meant for people who absolutely need every ounce of performance no matter the cost. We don't talk about Titan cards for the same reason we frankly shouldn't talk about the 3090 class, unless we're properly adjusting for current price and ignoring MSRP.

Ultimately, the best thing you can say about this card is that, at MSRP, it slots in about where you'd expect. But that's more or less what the 2000 series did and everyone hated that. Despite performance improvements, prices went up to match, so the only thing actually "worth" getting this time around is the absolute top-tier with the 4090, because everything else is, at best, "shave off 30% performance to save 30% cash".

This confirms that the last GPU series Nvidia released that made sense price wise was the GTX 1000 series, with the GTX 1080 as top dog. I've been PC gaming since Ultima Online, and I never had an issue with spending the equiv of a console (or a little bit more) on a GPU as long as I could get the top end, or close to the top end card of that series. It was a perfect trade off. Pay more money for the card vs a console, build the PC around that card, come out more expensive than a console (obviously), but have 3x-4x MORE graphical fidelity vs the newest console gen that will in turn outlive two console generations easily. If you built it yourself, you could do this for around $1000 to $1200 for a complete top of line Nvidia/Intel PC build. Load up a game, crank up all settings to Ultra w/o thinking about anything else, and play.

Now these prices make no sense. Its a joke. These top end, and even mid range GPUs are the price of entire top end PC builds. AMD is the only one who even makes close to sense price wise anymore, and even they are getting up there in price each series. You can argue that people just need to "get with the times!" and "inflation!" when it comes to these new prices, but when prices almost DOUBLED in 1 generation, add in scalpers on top of that, and consoles are STILL around $500-$600 10-15 years later, it really makes you wonder wtf is the point.

comments.text:
@Leynad778  This is not a 4090 review. 

The only game where I've found RT to actually make a significant difference appreciable during gameplay was Control. In most games the effect is either too subtle or implemented as more of a tech demo. 

Yes, there are videos on it. LTT themselves have done a video on RT where in a blind test many couldn't tell if RT is on or off, they actually had to stop playing and very closely examine a scene. And that's a common theme. In most games you can only really tell in very specific scenes under some lighting conditions, which you will hardly ever appreciate while gaming. 
To make things worse, RT makes some scenes look dull and uninteresting, even if more realistic. We've spent several decades trying to figure out how to make lighting look good without RT, it'll take a while before we start making games where RT makes the whole game look much better compared to pure raster. And until we do, 40+% performance hit will not be even remotely justifiable unless it's at 100+ FPS natively.

I think, one problem is, to push the old generations out of the market, the price of the new generation must be attractive. Prices are high and that leaves room for older generation cards that still have a good performance (or performance-cost ratio). If the 40 series cards would be a little cheaper, people would consider buying them and the price for a 30 series card would drop a little faster. that would create more pressure on the 20 series etc. Of course, only if there are enough cards of a better series available. But with this high prices, there is plenty of room for every budget. 
A cheaper 30* would even be more attractive to buy. But for a person with a certain budget, it would be interesting to buy a 40* card that today maybe is too expensive. The demand for 30 gen cards would slowly drop, and the demand (and price) for 20 gen cards even faster. Especially professional dealers have to think about how low they can push the price for an older card, if they could sell the newest generation for a better price.

I have trouble complaining about high GPU prices for "mid-tier" cards today. The newest generation of cards are incredibly powerful, both in terms of performance and watts guzzled down their pipes. As shown in the review, the 4070 Ti is roughly comparable to last generation's **90 series.

On one hand, I am an enthusiast at heart. More power! More frames! Let's goooo!

But on the other, what I actually want and need is a proper low power, low cost "budget" market that gives me room to grow, but also sets me up to play fun games and bring productivity boosts to old systems via CUDA or OpenCL acceleration.

This is what makes the Steam Deck attractive to me, and, perhaps more attractive still, is one of the latest generation AMD based mini PCs which I can get for about the same price as just one of the cards on review in today's video.

An entire PC which I can eventually reinstall with SteamOS for the TV, or repurpose into a PfSense or OpnSense router? Count me in, at least in comparison to the rest of this god awful market.

Perhaps this long winded rant is just to say... Maybe I'm just tired of everyone trying to keep up with the Joneses. Maybe what I really want is to play games, and do useful things with my computers. And for the most part, the hardware is capable of making this happen, if only one of these companies takes it seriously.
comments.author: @MattZietzkeXXIII

comments.text:
As a side note (hence a new reply) another very attractive aspect of going for a mini PC is that many productivity suites can be setup with tools for local "cloud" computation, offloading workloads such as rendering to multiple devices in the home for greater performance.

Flamenco v3 for Blender is a great example of this, and a tool I'm using myself to make better use of all the hardware I have available. While I'm no 3D artist, Blender is a hobby that I enjoy, and I have a lot to learn in this space. I can now do exactly that from any of my devices, my Dell XPS 13 laptop with crappy intel integrated graphics included.

Adding a mini PC to this mix would give me a huge uplift in rendering compute performance, even while satisfying many of my other needs and wants, and giving me multiple potential paths for reusing the hardware down the line, as mentioned in the root comment of this thread.

I think there's something special and valuable in this line of thinking, and it's a perspective I don't see shared by many others. That's the only reason why I'm commenting here at all. Hopefully I'm not just talking nonsense here.

comments.text: Here is how I look at the pricing.  Nvidia has the muscle to set its own MSRP, board partners' suggestions be damned.  There are several board partners that buy both Nvidia and AMD GPUs to make their own value-added cards.  The last thing these board partners want is for AMD to come in with an $800 RX Radeon 7900 XTX and $600 RX Radeon 7900 XT, because all that money these board partners paid to Nvidia to offer the RTX 40 series cards will be sitting on a shelf while the Radeon 7000 series variant is selling.  Those board partners want to supply both cards to the market, and get their share of the pie.  Meanwhile, AMD is not in the same position as Nvidia to muscle board partners into an MSRP.  As such, AMD is more prone to accept board partners' suggestions on MSRP so they are able to sell through their inventory of both Nvidia and AMD line-ups.  Otherwise, the board partners would be more committed to Nvidia because they believe Nvidia will sell thanks to the fanbase, well according to market "research", and tell AMD to make their own OC cards.  AMD would be lucky in that case if they pull off a Nintendo Wii.

comments.text: I'd say instead of pushing gamers to consoles, NVIDIA more likely expects to push gamers to laptops and hope that its board partners simply decide to quietly exit stage left on their own, leaving more of the desktop AIB market to the Founder's Edition business. The way I see it, NVIDIA simply wants more money out of its consumers, to the point where their AIB partners are looking more like obstacles to the objective instead of stepping stones, but they can't just abruptly cut them off, especially not when some of those AIBs have an OEM style desktop/laptop business going that NVIDIA still wants a presence in. So instead, they squeeze them out slowly on GPU die pricing and let business economics handle the rest - some might drop out like EVGA, some may pivot to being AMD or Intel exclusive (like PowerColor I think?) but most will simply increase the desktop card SKU pricing to keep the margin healthy and just redirect some supply to laptops as needed. And this will probably work for a while anyway given that Intel is still a very new entrant and AMD has much less marketshare in laptops. Note how NVIDA's laptop RTX 40 series announcement includes a laptop 4060, but there's no desktop 4060 announcement yet.

As cyberpunk runs at 50-ish fps, DLSS 3 needs to generate 5p-ish frames per second.  But as F1 runs at 110+ fps, it needs to generate 110+ frames to get a 100% performance uplift. 
I suspect that the reduced tensor core count limits the amount of frames DLSS 3 can generate. Given the numbers, the 4070ti seems to be able to generate only 80-90 additional frames per second at 4K, regardless of the title

comments.text:
The flaws in your price argument: 

1) For a gamer, these latest generation products are luxury items and cannot be described any other way. Price is always going to be what the market can bare plus a luxury tax. Standard consumer products are what the market can bare, luxury items such as sports cars, fancy watches, shoes, fancy screwdrivers and backpacks, and latest gen GPUs are what the market can bare plus the swag tax, because no one needs them and there are more affordable alternatives. 

2) What would be a fair price? Well that depends on who you ask. Youtubers can't agree. GN would probably say like $4-500 (Steve seems to think everything should cost what previous hardware cost). HUB has stated $700. Jay maybe $750 because he usually seems to be a bit more tolerant of higher prices. I personally would like to see this at about $600. No matter what was agreed upon, there'd still be complaining because it'd be out of reach of someone who wants it. The point is if we can't agree on what a fair price is, how can we expect to Nvidia to provide one? So we're back to point 1, it's what the market can bare... plus the swag tax of buying into the latest and greatest.

Also not a fan of the console argument. I've personally converted at least a dozen people in the past year from PS4 and PS5's and Xboxes, with PC's that don't use any of these parts you're complaining about prices for. It doesn't take much to impress a console user, a 12100 paired with a 1650 is usually enough even on their old TV they used for said console, before you even get to actual gaming monitors, and those builds come out around the same price.

P.S. Rethink the picture on the thumbnail. I'm assuming the goal was angry Linus and yeah it doesn't hit the mark.

What makes me laugh is that the rtx 2000 didn't even get the opportunity to shine a 4 year old architecture. 
Like really. 
Those gpu are compatible with dx12 ultimate. 
( dx12 ultimate = sfs + direct storage) 
And mesh shading 
I suspect a massive performance uplift for the games using those Microsoft tech.

And to extremely real here,
I can't imagine a studios saying no scalability. 

What I mean Is for them making their dream games without feeling the need to snap back to reality just because lower end gpus wouldn't keep up .
An since the goal of a studios is to make a ton of money,  concessions in game design are more often than not required. 


Unfortunately there is too many people rocking a gtx 1000 thanks to amd fsr 😑. 

Amd isn't the only culprit .
Ps4 and xbox one don't help either. 

There is a fair amount of money to be made when delivering a game on those hardware. 
Meaning taking in account the biggest bottleneck in history,  you name it... the hard drive 🥳.

When your a small independent studios,  your priorities are to establish a trust between you and your audience. 
On top of get the most bang for the buck.
Even if it means making hard cut in ideas because of hard-drive poor streaming capabilities. 

On thing that is nice  is that ssd are getting cheaper  .
The ps4 and xbox one are the last thing forcing the devs to use a pipeline dedicated to hard-drive when everyone else has a ssd or even a sata at minimum .

Finally ssd will be more than a convenience product. 
Really,  ssd of today are just there make loading time faster and Nothing more.

Studios will at last create a pipeline around ssd streaming capabilities in the i/o.
A constant flux of data basically making the gpu and cpu work faster so boosting raw performance by a lot.

When I say "boosting raw performance "
I just meant making the gpu and cpu at close to their limits.
And sfs,direct-storage + mesh shading will push the barrier further. 

The gpus compatible with dx 12 ultimate are 
Rtx 2000,3000,4000
Rx 6000,7000 , xbox series. 

It won't be too long before all owners of gtx 1000  get one of these gpu .
